In this study, the decadal prediction skill for the NAO and the interactions with the underlying ocean are assessed in retrospective forecasts spanning 1960–2020 using eight different decadal prediction systems (DPSs) and observation-based data.

Evidence is shown that NAO skill is related to positive feedback between subpolar SSTs and the NAO, which varies in strength between DPSs yet may still be too weak even in the most skillful systems compared to an observational estimate.

We also report evidence that the positive feedback is opposed by a delayed negative feedback between the NAO and the ocean circulation, which is used to further explain the disparities in NAO skill across systems.
Our findings, therefore, suggest that North Atlantic ocean-atmosphere interactions are central to NAO decadal predictability.

Such variations in the NAO have significant climate impacts, especially over Europe, via associated changes in the extratropical jet stream 9 , 10 , and hence society may profoundly benefit from skillful predictions of the NAO.

However, questions remain regarding the mechanisms underlying NAO predictability, particularly on the decadal timescale 5 , 8 .

Previous studies suggest that the decadal predictability of the NAO, as demonstrated in retrospective forecasts of the last few decades 7 , 8 , 12 , 13 , may arise from its interactions with the North Atlantic 8 , 14 .

However, the precise mechanisms governing the influence of North Atlantic SST anomalies on the extratropical atmospheric circulation are not fully understood, partly because the extratropical atmospheric response to midlatitude SST anomalies is obscured by the strong internal variability of the extratropical atmosphere 19 , and partly because simulated atmospheric responses in model experiments seemingly depend on the specific model and resolution that is used 20 – 22 .

However, the precise mechanisms governing the influence of North Atlantic SST anomalies on the extratropical atmospheric circulation are not fully understood, partly because the extratropical atmospheric response to midlatitude SST anomalies is obscured by the strong internal variability of the extratropical atmosphere 19 , and partly because simulated atmospheric responses in model experiments seemingly depend on the specific model and resolution that is used 20 – 22 .
The relationship between the North Atlantic and the decadal NAO signal may also be viewed as a two-way interaction, as the NAO is known to drive oceanic variability through various processes 23 .

Most notably, the NAO affects the upper-ocean via surface heat flux anomalies (latent, sensible, and radiative), yielding red-noise variability in SSTs due to the ocean mixed-layer’s large heat capacity 24 , 25 .
For example, surface heat fluxes associated with the positive phase of the NAO cool the subpolar North Atlantic region 25 – 27 .
The NAO may also influence oceanic variability on long timescales via its impacts on ocean circulation 26 , 28 .

Specifically, NAO-related surface wind-stress anomalies can drive delayed responses of the ocean gyres that evolve on annual timescales 28 , 29 , and NAO-related surface heat flux anomalies can drive delayed responses in the subpolar North Atlantic gyre and Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) that evolve on decadal timescales 30 – 32 .

Whether such mechanisms are relevant to decadal NAO variability in the real world remains to be determined, in large part due to the limited observational record of the ocean circulation and an incomplete understanding of the ocean’s influence on the NAO.

We further show that this deficiency is related to both parts of the feedback loop: the atmospheric response to subpolar SSTs, but also the response of the underlying ocean to the NAO.

The results are also consistent with previous studies showing a link between North Atlantic SSTs and the NAO signal in hindcasts 8 , 14 and other studies showing that climate models tend to underestimate multidecadal variability in North Atlantic SSTs and the extratropical atmospheric circulation 39 – 42 in association with an underestimated ocean-atmosphere connection 42 , 43 .

The results are also consistent with previous studies showing a link between North Atlantic SSTs and the NAO signal in hindcasts 8 , 14 and other studies showing that climate models tend to underestimate multidecadal variability in North Atlantic SSTs and the extratropical atmospheric circulation 39 – 42 in association with an underestimated ocean-atmosphere connection 42 , 43 .

This is supported by previous studies showing more generally that North Atlantic SST anomalies can impact the eddy-driven jet via their impact on meridional gradients in low-level baroclinicity 8 , 15 – 18 .

However, model experiments also show that the simulated extratropical atmospheric response to North Atlantic SST anomalies depends on the model that is used, with some responses projecting more strongly onto the NAO than others 20 , 21 .

Understanding the causes of model disparities in the atmospheric response to North Atlantic SST anomalies is a challenging task, yet may be key to understanding why DPSs seemingly under-represent the positive feedback between subpolar SSTs and the NAO.

Deficiencies in the simulated patterns of internal variability in the atmosphere (e.g., related to the NAO and/or blocking) and the ocean (the AMOC, the Gulf Stream, and the wind-driven ocean gyres) may also adversely affect the feedback.

Further targeted multi-model studies are needed to pin down the origins of model deficiencies in the extratropical atmospheric circulation response to North Atlantic SST anomalies and the associated positive feedback.

Since the delayed subpolar warming opposes the initial subpolar cooling that acts to reinforce positive NAO anomalies, we argue that the AMOC acts as a delayed negative feedback to the NAO, consistent with previous studies 56 , 60 , 66 .

This different AMOC behavior may be related to disparities in ocean initialization and/or the AMOC response to the NAO between the two groups of DPSs, but this should be investigated in future studies.

Although the AMOC appears to play a key role here, other aspects of the ocean circulation may be relevant to NAO predictability and should be explored further, particularly the gyre response to wind-stress anomalies associated with the NAO 55 , 57 , 67 .

Regardless of whether the decadal variability is internally or externally driven, our findings emphasize the importance of ocean initialization and the accurate representation of two-way ocean-NAO interactions in producing skillful decadal predictions of the NAO.

The hindcasts were performed by eight different DPSs from the Decadal Climate Prediction Project contribution to phase 6 of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6), referred to as the dcppA-hindcast experiments 44 .

To produce the decadal hindcasts, model simulations were realistically initialized every November (except for CanESM and IPSL, which were initialized in January, and NorCPM, which was initialized in October) and then run for 10 years.
We also formed 60-member ensembles for the skill-less DPS by combining all members from the IPSL, MIROC, CanESM, EC-Earth and NorCPM DPSs.
To isolate decadal variability, the NAO index was smoothed with an 8-year running average.
In this case, we resample with replacement the fields or indices being tested in 5-year blocks in order to account for autocorrelation.

In this way, the IMC reflects a unique time evolution of a given field or index that is based on a single member and hence facilitates a fair comparison with results from the single realization of ERA5.
